passage: Harsha, you asked why I'm up till midnight, so here it is. I'm Uday. I found this speaker online in the summer, and his videos make life feel clear. He talks about waking early, being kind, having a purpose, and for the first time I feel like someone explains why I get up. I've watched every video, some twice. Last week you sent me a talk by a different speaker on the same idea, and they disagreed on one point. That bothered me at first, then I liked it. Now I keep a note of what each video asks me to do: wake early, help at home, nothing about money. I still like him. I just compare now.

qa.q: When did Uday find the speaker online?
qa.a: Uday found the speaker in the summer.

qa.q: What is Uday feeling about the speaker, and what shows it?
qa.a: Uday admires the speaker; watching every video, some twice, and feeling that life is clear show it. 🙂

qa.q: What is the benefit of Uday's habit of noting what each video asks?
qa.a: It lets Uday compare speakers and see what is being asked, such as habits and not money, so enjoying the videos does not turn into blind following.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uday's late nights and the different talk Harsha sent?
qa.a: Harsha probably cares and wanted Uday to hear another view, and Uday's reaction shows Harsha's suggestion was welcome.

grounding: Uday admires an online speaker who makes life feel clear, and enjoys the videos while comparing sources and noting what they ask.

passage: On the bus to the kasba school, Nirmala played the preacher's talk on one earphone and ignored the chatter. "He says most people are lost," Nirmala told Tenzin. "He has the answer to everything." Tenzin raised an eyebrow. "Everything?" At the momo stall after school, a thought arrived: Tenzin was lost, and so were the two girls at the next table. Nirmala noticed how the thought felt: cold. That night Nirmala searched for the figure the preacher had quoted about villages and found a different number from the district office. Nirmala frowned and saved a note: ask Tenzin's aunt, the teacher. On Saturday Nirmala went to Tenzin's mother's shop as usual.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala listen to the preacher's talk?
qa.a: Nirmala listened on the bus to the kasba school, with one earphone.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel on noticing the thought that Tenzin was lost?
qa.a: Nirmala felt uneasy; the thought felt cold, and it sent Nirmala to check the preacher's figure.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do so that one voice does not take over?
qa.a: Keep checking claims against other sources, ask a trusted teacher such as Tenzin's aunt, and keep friends like Tenzin.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel about being described among the lost?
qa.a: Probably puzzled or dismissed; Tenzin's raised eyebrow and "Everything?" show doubt, though Tenzin was not told directly.

grounding: Nirmala starts to think a preacher has all answers and others are lost, then checks a claim and keeps friends.

passage:
Counsellor's note. Pranav came to see me after class, quiet and pale. Pranav said an online preacher tells followers that families who "cling" are chains, and asks each follower for a monthly donation from pocket money, and to say nothing to parents. Pranav said, "I feel guilty when I don't send it, and scared something bad will happen." Pranav had stopped eating with the cousins and felt lonely. I explained calmly that real guidance does not ask for secrecy, money or distance from family. I asked if we could tell Pranav's parents together. After a long silence Pranav agreed. I phoned Pranav's mother that afternoon.
- Vidya, school counsellor

qa.q: What did the preacher ask Pranav to keep from the parents?
qa.a: The preacher asked Pranav to say nothing to the parents about the monthly donation.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling, and what showed it?
qa.a: Pranav felt guilty, scared and lonely; the fear that something bad would happen if the money was not sent and the stopped meals with the cousins show it.

qa.q: What did Vidya do to help, and why does it work?
qa.a: Vidya explained that guidance which demands secrecy, money or distance is not real guidance, and brought in the parents, so a trusted adult can help. 🤍

qa.q: How might Pranav's parents feel on hearing this?
qa.a: Probably worried, but also relieved that Pranav told someone; the note only says that Vidya phoned Pranav's mother.

grounding: A preacher uses guilt, fear and secrecy to get Pranav's money and distance from family; a counsellor helps Pranav recognise it and involve parents.

passage:
Monday. "He's a fraud, Papa. Everyone can see it." Lokesh switched off the speaker's talk. "You don't know anything about him." Shankar left the room with a hot face, and neither ate much.
Wednesday. Shankar sat beside Lokesh on the sofa. "What do you like in his talks? I really want to know." Lokesh paused. "After a long day at work, they help me feel patient. I need that." Shankar nodded. "Okay. That I can see."
Saturday. "One thing bothers me, Papa. He asked people to give money for a hall, and I couldn't find any accounts. I'm not calling him a liar. Can we look together?" Lokesh sighed. "Fair. Bring the laptop."

qa.q: What does Lokesh say the talks help with?
qa.a: Lokesh says they help with feeling patient after a long day at work.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling on Monday, and how did it change by Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday Shankar was frustrated and doubtful, with a hot face; by Wednesday Shankar was curious enough to ask what Papa likes in the talks.

qa.q: What worked better than calling the preacher a fraud?
qa.a: Asking what Lokesh finds helpful and then raising one specific concern, about the hall money, kindly and without ridicule.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt when Shankar first called the preacher a fraud?
qa.a: Probably defensive and hurt, since Lokesh switched off the talk and said "You don't know anything about him".

grounding: Shankar argues with a parent about a preacher, then asks what the parent finds helpful and shares a specific concern without ridicule.

passage:
Tuesday. Swati shoved her phone across the desk. "Read this." A report said the preacher told followers to give up luxuries, while he lived in a big house and took money from their donations. Neelam read it twice and felt heat in the face. "I sent him my pocket money."
Thursday. Neelam deleted every saved video, jaw tight. "I feel so stupid. And so angry." Swati said, "You were hoping. That's not stupid."
Sunday. Neelam sat on the terrace, thinking of one talk about being patient with others. It had helped her with her little brother. She kept that note and thought, that part was true anyway.

qa.q: What did Neelam find out about how the preacher lived?
qa.a: Neelam found that the preacher told followers to give up luxuries while living in a big house and taking money from their donations.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling on Thursday, and why?
qa.a: Neelam felt stupid and angry, since Neelam had sent the preacher pocket money and now saw the gap between his words and his life.

qa.q: What could Neelam keep from the teachings?
qa.a: The parts that proved true in life, such as patience with others, which helped with Neelam's little brother, while dropping the rest.

qa.q: How does Swati see Neelam's hope?
qa.a: Swati does not think it was stupid; she says "You were hoping", so hope itself was not the mistake.

grounding: Neelam discovers the preacher lives against his own words and earns from followers, feels foolish and angry, and keeps the teachings that were true.

passage:
First Monday. Joseph skipped Saturday football and said, "The people outside my group are asleep." Anjali kept her voice warm. "What do you like about it? I'd like to understand." Joseph talked for an hour, glowing.
Two weeks later. Joseph stopped answering messages and left the class chat. Anjali noticed Joseph no longer ate with the cousins either. She waited at the gate and said, "I miss you. You don't have to explain anything." Joseph gave a small nod and left.
That Friday, Anjali told the school counsellor everything, including how Joseph had been cut off from everyone. It felt like a risk to the friendship, but Anjali stayed beside Joseph at the counsellor's door.

qa.q: What did Joseph stop doing on the first Monday?
qa.a: Joseph skipped Saturday football.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling by the final scene, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anjali felt worried but loyal; telling the counsellor, even though it felt like a risk, and staying beside Joseph at the door show it. 🤍

qa.q: Why did Anjali tell an adult even though Joseph might be upset?
qa.a: Joseph had been cut off from friends and cousins and had gone silent, so a trusted adult was needed; friendship alone was not enough.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Anjali's warm questions?
qa.a: Possibly as care rather than mockery, though Joseph still pulled away, so Anjali cannot be sure how it landed.

grounding: A friend changes after being pulled into an extreme online group; Anjali stays warm, asks questions and involves a counsellor when Joseph is cut off.

passage: Devika, you asked why I keep the old group chat but never post. I'm Wasim, and at fifteen I felt invisible at home. Abba worked nights and nobody asked about my day. Then an online community began greeting me by name every morning and saying they were glad I was there. That warmth was real, and I won't pretend it wasn't. I nearly moved my whole life into it. But one night I asked myself: does being welcome make everything they teach true? I couldn't say yes. So I joined the school cricket club, made two friends who could sit beside me, and kept the chat as one small part of my days.

qa.q: How old was Wasim when the online community began greeting Wasim by name?
qa.a: Wasim was fifteen.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling at home, and why did the community appeal?
qa.a: Wasim felt invisible at home, so a community greeting Wasim by name every morning felt warm and welcome. 🙂

qa.q: What offline step did Wasim take?
qa.a: Wasim joined the school cricket club and made two friends who could sit beside Wasim, keeping the chat as one small part of life.

qa.q: What would probably have been different if Wasim had felt seen at home?
qa.a: The pull of an online welcome would likely have been weaker, since Wasim would not have felt so invisible.

grounding: Wasim feels unseen at home and is warmly welcomed by an online community, finds the warmth real but not proof of truth, and builds offline friendships.

passage: The school bus rattled through heavy rain, and there were twenty minutes left before the chemistry test. Madhav noticed the sticker on Darshan's bag and laughed. "Still backing that leader? Good luck with that." Darshan's face burned. A sharp insult was ready on the tongue. Darshan breathed in three times, then asked, "What do you mean by that?" Madhav's grin faded. "My uncle's shop closed after a decision people say came from that side. It's not about you." Darshan hadn't known. "I still see it differently," Darshan said, "but I'm sorry about the shop." The bus turned into the school gate, and they walked in without another word.

qa.q: What was about to happen in twenty minutes?
qa.a: A chemistry test.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when Madhav laughed, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Darshan felt angry; the burning face and the sharp insult ready on the tongue show it.

qa.q: What could Darshan try next time the topic comes up?
qa.a: Pause, breathe, and ask what the other person means before answering, keeping the person separate from the view.

qa.q: What might Madhav's laugh mean from Madhav's side?
qa.a: It may come from the pain of the uncle's shop closing rather than from dislike of Darshan; Madhav says "It's not about you".

grounding: Someone mocks the leader Darshan supports; Darshan flares up, then pauses and asks what Madhav means instead of insulting.

passage: Shalini, you said your classmates on the other side are just idiots. Sit, and let me tell you what I once thought. I'm Lalremsiami, and at sixteen I was sure everyone who disagreed with my side in the school debate was stupid, or worse. It felt good, like standing on high ground. It was also lonely: I ate lunch alone and my messages went quiet. Then my teacher paired me with Zothan, from the other side, for a project. He brought tea and asked about my grandmother's weaving before he said a word about politics. I still disagreed with him. But I couldn't call him stupid anymore. I hold my views more gently now.

qa.q: Who did Lalremsiami's teacher pair Lalremsiami with for the project?
qa.a: The teacher paired Lalremsiami with Zothan.

qa.q: Why did contempt feel good to Lalremsiami, and what did it cost?
qa.a: It felt like standing on high ground, but it cost Lalremsiami friendship: lunch alone and quiet messages. 😊

qa.q: What could Shalini try after hearing this?
qa.a: Notice the stereotype of the other side and talk with one real person from it, holding views with some humility.

qa.q: How might Zothan have seen Lalremsiami at the start?
qa.a: Probably as a stiff classmate from the other side, yet Zothan still brought tea and asked about the grandmother's weaving.

grounding: Lalremsiami recalls seeing the other side as stupid, feeling good and lonely, then meeting one real person from that side.

passage: Yusuf lingered after computer class until the lab emptied. "Sir, can I show you something?" The phone held dozens of comments under a post about a school debate: cruel words about Yusuf's opinion, then about Yusuf's religion. "I typed a reply," Yusuf said quietly, "and deleted it. I blocked two of them, but I took screenshots first." Abhinav Sir read slowly, jaw tight. "Thank you for showing me. Disagreeing is fine. This is cruelty, and it is not your fault." He sent the screenshots to the school head and offered to phone Yusuf's father with Yusuf beside him. Yusuf's shoulders dropped for the first time that day.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do before blocking two of the commenters?
qa.a: Yusuf took screenshots first.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when lingering after class, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Yusuf was hurt and anxious; the quiet voice and the shoulders dropping in relief afterwards show it.

qa.q: Why was it sensible for Yusuf not to reply in kind?
qa.a: Replying would feed the cruelty, while blocking, saving proof and telling a trusted adult protects Yusuf and gives the school something to act on.

qa.q: How does Abhinav Sir see the comments?
qa.a: As cruelty, not disagreement, and not Yusuf's fault; he says so and reports it to the school head.

grounding: Yusuf is abused online for an opinion and religion, saves proof, blocks, does not reply in kind and tells a trusted teacher.
